segment: More than one year, all students
applies_to: all undergraduates (College of Arts and Sciences); international students whose first language is not English are exempt
level_required: Proficiency equivalent to the 201 level: 'World language proficiency, whether in a modern or classical language, is a requirement for all Lewis & Clark students.' Met by a passing grade in a world or classical language course at the 201 level (on campus or on an approved overseas program), by an ACTFL score equivalent to 201 in both speaking and writing (modern languages), or by meeting SCS guidelines equivalent to 201 in reading and translation (classical languages).
test_out: Placement exam: 'by placing into 202 or above on a language placement examination for a language other than English' (the exam must be from a regionally accredited institution). Exemption for international students whose first language is not English. U.S. citizens with non-English proficiency from living abroad must take a regionally accredited placement exam (registrar advises on alternatives if none exists for the language). AP/IB scores and high-school years are not stated on the general education page.
notes: Listed as the 'World Language' section of the General Education Requirements (2026-27 Undergraduate Catalog, graduationrequirements/generaleducation). The HTML page's World Language tab did not render for fetching; the text was read from the catalog's PDF version of the same section. Separate 'Global Perspectives' general education requirement is a culture/perspectives course requirement and is distinct from the World Language proficiency requirement; the catalog notes language-acquisition courses need registrar intervention to be applied to Global Perspectives.

applies_to: College of Arts and Sciences students only (all bachelor's degrees offered by the College of Arts and Sciences, B.A. and B.S.); not part of the University Core, so students in Business, Engineering, Nursing/Human Physiology, and Education have no language requirement
level_required: 'Language Requirement: Competency in a second language (classical or modern) at the intermediate level (demonstrated by completion of a course numbered 201 or higher) is required for students continuing in the study of a language. Students beginning study in a language they have not previously studied can fulfill the requirement by completing one year at the beginning level (courses numbered 101-102).'
test_out: Automatic fulfillment for 'international students from non-English speaking countries whose primary and/or secondary education was in a language other than English.' The gonzaga.edu CAS requirements page adds that non-native English speakers who have completed the required English core credits may petition the Associate Dean of Arts and Sciences for a waiver. No placement-exam, AP/IB, or high-school-years test-out is stated; continuing students are placed and must reach 201.
notes: Two-track structure: students continuing a previously studied language must reach the intermediate level (201), while students starting a new language need only the 101-102 year, so the minimum for a no-background student is two semesters. Languages regularly offered: Filipino, French, German, Greek, Italian, Japanese, Latin, Spanish (gonzaga.edu page also lists Arabic, ASL, Chinese). ITAL 105/106 do not fulfill the requirement. The gonzaga.edu/catalogs page lists 2025-2026 as the current undergraduate catalog (catalog.gonzaga.edu); the www.gonzaga.edu/catalogs/current CAS page gives slightly different wording ('courses numbered 201-202') and was used for the waiver detail.

applies_to: n/a - no college-wide language requirement; any foreign language requirement is 'a matter left to the discretion of the departments and divisions' (set by some majors, e.g., in the Division of Literature and Languages)
level_required: None. The eight graduation requirements (units, distribution requirements including Humanities 110, PE/experiential, major, divisional, junior qual, senior thesis, senior oral) include no language requirement; language courses appear only as one option within Group I (Humanities and the Arts) of the distribution requirements, with the rule that 'no more than two units in Group I can be from language classes or from literature classes.'
test_out: n/a
notes: Confirmed in the 2024-25 catalog (reed.edu/catalog/edu_program.html), the 2022-23 archived catalog (which states the foreign language requirement is left to departments and divisions), the Reed Guidebook degree-requirements page, and the Registrar's degree-requirements page. The Division of History and Social Sciences divisional requirements contain no language requirement; the Division of Literature and Languages page could not be fetched (robots). Discrepancy: Reed's 2025-26 Common Data Set section E3 appears to mark 'Foreign languages' as an area required of all or most students, which does not match the catalog's stated requirements; the catalog was treated as authoritative. Reed's new catalog site (catalog.reed.edu, 2026-27) could not be read; no indication was found that a language requirement was added.

segment: More than one year, some students
applies_to: College of Arts and Sciences B.A. candidates only; the CAS B.S. college requirements (6 credit hours: Effective Communication and Commitment and Consciousness) have no language requirement, and the University Core has none
level_required: 'Language Requirement (3-12 credit hours): At least one language course other than English' with progression 'through the 202-level in French, German, or Spanish' or 'the 103/113-level in Chinese.'
test_out: Not stated in the Bulletin beyond 'Any exceptions to the language requirement must be approved by the Office of the Dean' of the College together with the Department of International Languages and Cultures. The wording 'at least one language course' implies a course is required regardless of placement; placement tests (French and Spanish via Moodle; German and Chinese by consultation) set the starting level. No AP/IB or high-school-years rule stated.
notes: Four-semester sequence (101-102-201-202) for French/German/Spanish; the Chinese track ends at the 103/113 level (three courses), so the minimum varies by language. The 3-12 credit-hour range reflects students who place high and need only one course. A 300-level language course can also count toward the 15-credit upper-division requirement. The University Core Curriculum (all UP undergraduates) has no language component; the CAS 'Commitment and Consciousness' requirement is a Diversity or Global & Historical Consciousness course, not a language course.

applies_to: all undergraduates (Language core is part of the University Core required for the baccalaureate degree), with exemptions for students whose high school instruction was not in English and reductions for heritage learners and AP/IB scorers
level_required: 'Two courses are required for all students' (Language Core, 0-2 units) in Chinese, French, German, Greek, Japanese, Latin, or Spanish, taught in the target language; no minimum course level is stated (a student with no background would take the two elementary courses). Courses numbered x00-x09 count only toward the Language Core; x10-x89 count toward both Language Core and the Arts & Humanities division.
test_out: Students whose high school diploma is from a school where the primary language of instruction was not English 'do not need to take further courses.' Heritage learners take only one course. Students with an AP language score of 4 or 5, or an IB higher-level language score of 5, 6, or 7, take only one course. Transfer credit may fulfill one or both courses (each approved transfer course must be at least 4 quarter or 3 semester credits). No placement-exam test-out is stated for the current (2023-24 and later) Language Core; students on the 2022-23 Bulletin or earlier could use a Language Proficiency Exam.
notes: The Language Core was revised in 2023-24 from a proficiency-based requirement to a two-course requirement. The 2026-27 Bulletin (bulletin.pugetsound.edu/policy/undergraduateprograms) lists 'Language requirement' among the core requirements and links to LANG-attribute courses; the detailed rules are on the university's Language Core Requirement page. The page also lists a small set of approved English-taught courses that count toward the Language Core (ARTH 371, CONN 330, FREN 391, GERM 350, GERM 355, GERM 392, GLAM 120), so the requirement can in principle be met without language-acquisition coursework. Credit/no-credit courses do not fulfill it.

applies_to: students in menu option: all undergraduates must take at least three credits in the 'Global Cultures and Languages' Explorations category, which can be satisfied by a language course OR a non-language global-cultures course
level_required: No proficiency level. The General Studies program (Fall 2024 and later) requires 'at least three credits' in each of seven Explorations categories, one of which is 'Global Cultures and Languages' ('Language classes in particular examine how different cultures construct and communicate meaning through language'). A single language course of any level satisfies the category.
test_out: n/a for a stand-alone language requirement. For the distribution category: AP and IB credit do not count toward distribution requirements, and P-D-F (pass/fail) courses cannot be used.
notes: No stand-alone foreign-language graduation requirement appears in either the Degree Requirements page or the General Studies requirements. semesters_equivalent of 1 is the minimum if a student chooses a language course to fill the category; 0 if a culture course is chosen. Students who started before Fall 2024 follow the earlier General Studies program with a 'Cultural Pluralism' requirement (two courses, six credits), also not a language requirement.

applies_to: all Willamette College (undergraduate College of Arts and Sciences) students, including transfer students with AA/AS/AAOT degrees and dual-degree engineering students
level_required: Non-English Language (NEL) requirement, 8 credits: 'Complete the second semester (L132) or higher of a Willamette non-English language course with a minimum grade of C-' (i.e., 'All students are expected to study a language other than English through the 132 level').
test_out: Place into a 200-level language course on the placement exam and pass a proficiency exam administered on campus by Willamette faculty; complete the first year or higher of college-level study in one non-English language at another institution (transfer); AP language exam score of 4 or higher; IB higher-level language exam score of 5 or higher; or present evidence of a primary language other than English.
notes: The NEL requirement is the first half of the 16-credit 'World Engagement' general education component (2020 and later catalogs): 8 credits of NEL through 132, plus 8 additional credits from NEL study beyond 132, study abroad, Community-Engaged Learning, or Culture and Values courses. Students who satisfy the NEL requirement by placement/AP/IB still complete the 8 World Engagement elective credits, so World Engagement totals 8-16 credits depending on incoming language level. The 2026-27 catalog policy page (catalog.willamette.edu/pages/wJfjfr4OiO0IhZjAptNP) confirms the requirement for transfer students and lists AP/IB language exams as satisfying the non-English language requirement; the detailed wording quoted here is from the catalog's general education category page. A Foreign Language Requirement Substitution Policy for documented disabilities is handled by Accessible Education Services.

applies_to: all undergraduates ('All students will take a two course sequence in the same language'); international students whose native language is not English may petition the Academic Standing Committee for exemption
level_required: 'Non-Native Language (2 courses in sequence in the same language).' No proficiency level or course number is specified; the two sequential courses are taken at the level determined by the placement exam.
test_out: Effectively none: placing into a higher level on the language placement exam does not exempt a student, who still takes two sequential courses at that level (e.g., 201 then 202). 'AP Credit can be used for one of these courses' (AP score of 4 or 5 earns one course; one more course in the same language is then required; AP students still take the placement exam). Exemption by petition to the Academic Standing Committee / Registrar for students who learned in a language other than English during their last three years of secondary school. IB not stated on the curriculum pages.
notes: Part of the 'Perspectives & Social Change' component of the Gettysburg Curriculum (with Identities and Culture and Race, Power, and Equity). The requirement is course-based rather than proficiency-based, so every student completes two semesters regardless of prior background. Students who grew up bilingual but were schooled in English must still complete it (heritage speakers are placed appropriately). Detail on placement and AP comes from the Academic Advising 'Second Language Study' FAQ (gettysburg.edu/offices/x-academic-advising/faculty-resources/second-language-study/). Pre-Fall-2025 curriculum had a similar two-course language goal.

applies_to: all undergraduates ('All students consequently are required to demonstrate at least an intermediate-level proficiency' in a language other than English)
level_required: 'Demonstrated proficiency through the Intermediate Level (103 or 201, depending on the language)' - 'Up to 3 Units'; satisfied by completing 'the third language course (numbered 103 or 201, depending on the language)' in any sequence.
test_out: Placement exam: 'scoring at a proficiency level determined by the department on an examination developed or approved by the College.' AP/IB: 'see individual department policy' (varies by language). Students with at least two years of secondary education in a school teaching at least 50% of content in a language other than English may request certification through the Registrar. Partially bilingual students in a language not taught on campus may demonstrate intermediate-level literacy via an on-campus written essay test rated by a fluent speaker. Coursework in a language not offered at K may be taken at another institution with prior Registrar approval. Documented language learning disabilities handled through Disability Services.
notes: Kalamazoo runs on a quarter (three-term) calendar with one-unit courses; three sequential quarter courses (through 103, or 201 where the sequence is numbered differently) equal roughly one academic year of college language study, hence semesters_equivalent 2. Languages regularly offered: Chinese, French, German, Greek, Japanese, Latin, Spanish. Degree requirements table at kzoo.edu/catalog/curriculum/degree-requirements/ lists the requirement as 'Up to 3 Units'. The catalog site identifies itself as the 2025-2026 Academic Catalog.

applies_to: all undergraduates (all Kenyon students are candidates for the bachelor of arts degree)
level_required: students must demonstrate a level of proficiency in a second language equivalent to one full year of introductory college study
test_out: AP: 4 or 5 on Latin AP, or 3 or higher on any other second-language or literature AP exam; IB: 4 or higher on an HL or SL language exam; satisfactory score on the placement exam given during Orientation; transfer credit covering a year or more of study (final semester of a year-long sequence), approved in advance by the registrar and department chair; other documentation accepted by the registrar / Committee on Academic Standards (e.g., ACTFL Oral Proficiency Interview certificate, STAMP test); Kenyon Academic Partnership language credit. High-school years alone and native-speaker status are not listed as routes.
notes: Called the 'Second Language Requirement'. The coursework route is 'completing an introductory-level modern or classical language course at Kenyon'; Kenyon's introductory language courses are taught as a single year-long sequence (e.g., 111Y-112Y), so one course equals one full year (two semesters). The catalog notes a student cannot take the first semester elsewhere and finish with the second semester at Kenyon. Second-language courses may also count toward a diversification division. Separate from the Diversification requirement (1 unit in each of four divisions).

applies_to: all undergraduates (Core Program is required of all students; transfer students have the same Core requirements except First-Year Seminars)
level_required: All students must achieve Language 102-level proficiency in a language other than English (completion of Occidental's 102 course, a LANG-designated course, or an equivalent course at an accredited college or university)
test_out: Exemption-level score on Occidental's placement and/or exemption exam given during orientation; AP language exam score of 4 or above; SAT Subject Test: 560 or above in French, Spanish or Latin, 550 or above in German or Chinese, 540 or above in Japanese, 560 for other languages; proficiency exam for languages not taught at Occidental (contact Specialist for Language Education); international students who completed six or more years of elementary education in a non-English language are exempt (confirm with a language department chair). IB not mentioned. Transfer-equivalent courses accepted; online courses from other institutions do not count.
notes: The Foreign Language requirement is one component of the Core Program (First-Year Seminars; Culture: U.S. Diversity, Regional Focus, Global Connections; Arts and Pre-1800s; Science and Mathematics; Foreign Language). Students with more than one year of high-school study (grades 10-12) or more than one quarter of college in a language may not take 101 for credit and must take the placement exam. AP/IB generally cannot satisfy Core requirements; the language proficiency requirement is the stated exception. The Bachelor of Arts degree page lists 'Successful completion of the Core Program including the language proficiency requirement' among degree requirements, to be completed by end of junior year.

segment: More than one year, all students
applies_to: all undergraduates (candidates for both the B.A. and B.S. must complete the Foundation Requirements)
level_required: F10: 'Demonstrate intermediate second-language proficiency'; satisfied by successful completion of an appropriate four-credit course numbered 201 or higher (third semester), or by placing above 201 with approval of the language faculty
test_out: Placement test required for anyone with two or more years of high-school study in the language; placing above 201 plus faculty approval (face-to-face oral and written proficiency testing) satisfies F10; students who place into 202 or higher must consult the department. Greek/Latin: pass the Greek 201 or Latin 201 final/proficiency exam during Welcome Week; Hebrew: complete Hebrew 201 or pass its proficiency exam. AP 4/5 in Chinese, French, German, Spanish earns 201-level credit only if the student demonstrates proficiency above 201 (AP score alone does not satisfy F10); AP Latin 4/5 does not by itself satisfy F10. Transfer credit for a 201-level course accepted but proficiency must still be demonstrated. Languages not taught at Rhodes: petition for alternative proficiency testing before end of second year. Native-speaker status not addressed.
notes: The language requirement is Foundation F10 (not F8; F8 covers theory and empirical research). The Requirements for a Degree page notes 'the foreign language requirement may be satisfied by successful completion of a proficiency exam.' Students with fewer than two years of high-school study may begin at 101; students with two or more years may not take 101 for credit. Literature or culture courses taken in translation do not satisfy F10. Related pages: https://catalog.rhodes.edu/catalog/requirements-degree, https://catalog.rhodes.edu/educational-program/foundations-curriculum, https://www.rhodes.edu/academics/majors-minors/spanish/language-placement, https://www.rhodes.edu/ap-and-ib-credit.

applies_to: n/a
level_required: none
test_out: n/a
notes: Sarah Lawrence has no general education or core curriculum. B.A. degree requirements are 120 credits (at least 60 at Sarah Lawrence), residency, a minimum of 20 credits in lecture courses, and a distribution requirement: 'Degree candidates are required to complete a minimum of 10 credits in at least three of the four academic areas' (creative and performing arts; history and social sciences; humanities; natural sciences and mathematics), with caps per area and no more than 50 credits in a single discipline. Language appears only as a discipline within the humanities area; no foreign/world language course or proficiency is required. The 2026-27 handbook index URL given in the assignment returned a client error, so the 2025-26 handbook page was used; the undated 'undergraduate program planning' page at https://www.sarahlawrence.edu/student-life/student-handbook/undergraduate-academic-policies-procedures/undergraduate-program-planning.html carries the same policy.

applies_to: all undergraduates (Language Study is one of the four Foundations requirements all degree candidates must complete)
level_required: Language Study: a course that focuses on 'acquisition and/or analysis of a language other than English'; per the registrar's degree-requirements page, 'all students must complete one course in a foreign language. The course must be appropriate to your level of language expertise.'
test_out: None stated. The catalog says AP, IB and other testing-program credit 'may not count toward all-college requirements.' Placement determines the level of the one required course rather than exempting the student: students with prior knowledge of a modern language may not take 101 and must take the placement exam; students with advanced proficiency may meet the requirement with an upper-level literature/culture course taught in that language; heritage Spanish speakers take WLS 221; international students from non-English-speaking countries must still take a language course (Language Study FAQ).
notes: Skidmore's general education (introduced for students entering fall 2020) has Foundations (Expository Writing, Applied Quantitative Reasoning, Global Cultural Perspectives, Language Study), Inquiries (Artistic, Humanistic, Scientific) and Integrations (Scribner Seminar, Bridge Experience, Senior Experience Coda). Global Cultural Perspectives is a separate requirement that does not substitute for Language Study. Eligible languages: American Sign Language, Ancient Greek, Chinese, French, German, Hebrew, Korean, Italian, Japanese, Latin, Sanskrit, Spanish (WLL, Classics, Asian Studies). For self-instructional languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Portuguese, Russian, Korean) WLX-101 does not fulfill the requirement. Supporting pages: https://www.skidmore.edu/nsarg/degree-requirements.php, https://www.skidmore.edu/advising/documents/language-study-faq.pdf, https://www.skidmore.edu/world-languages-and-literatures/resources/requirements-and-placement.php.

segment: More than one year, all students
applies_to: all undergraduates (B.A. and B.M.; OLE Core requirement 'World Languages and Cultures', 0-3 courses depending on placement)
level_required: World Languages and Cultures (WLC): 'Depending on placement, proficiency, or transfer work, most incoming students will complete at least one course and a maximum of three courses at St. Olaf in order to fulfill the requirement.' Per St. Olaf's WLC description, the requirement is met by a 4th-semester-or-higher course (232) in French, German or Spanish, or a 3rd-semester-or-higher course (231) in Chinese, Greek, Japanese, Latin, Norwegian or Russian; students who begin French, German or Spanish at the first-semester course (111) need only complete the third-semester course (231).
test_out: Placement exam/survey sets the entry level (0-3 courses); students who place high may take the department's proficiency exam to fulfill WLC outright (e.g., Spanish Proficiency Exam). IB HL 7 in French/German/Spanish B: WLC awarded for passing the proficiency exam (or completing 25x as first course); IB HL 6: WLC awarded on completing 232; IB HL 5-7 Chinese: on completing CHIN 231; Greek/Latin HL 5-7: on completing 231. AP (older 2021 guide): score of 5 in French/German/Spanish may take the proficiency exam ('WLC will be awarded for passing proficiency exam'); score of 4 points to 232 (or 231 Chinese/Japanese), with WLC awarded for the course. Transfer work counts. Native-speaker status not addressed (international students who studied Spanish at home contact spanish-placement@stolaf.edu).
notes: WLC is listed at 0-3.00 credits for the B.A. and 0-2.00 for the B.M. B.M. exception: 'vocal performance majors must complete 112-level course in two languages, one of which is French or German.' A student starting a language from scratch needs three semesters (111, 112, 231) in every language; the 232 (fourth-semester) endpoint applies to French/German/Spanish students who enter above 111 via placement. Detailed WLC description from St. Olaf's Asian Studies page: https://wp.stolaf.edu/asian-studies/?p=4593 ; IB guide: https://wp.stolaf.edu/registrar/international-baccalaureate-exam-equivalency-guide-for-2026-27/ ; B.M. page: https://catalog.stolaf.edu/curriculum/graduate-requirements-degrees/ole-core-curric-bm-core/.

applies_to: students in menu option: World Languages (WOL) is one of the eight Perspectives in the Complex Questions: Global Challenges & Social Justice curriculum; students choose how to distribute their Perspectives courses
level_required: WOL Perspective: 'One term of a foreign language must be taken to fulfill this requirement' (entry-level or upper-level course; term-length language immersion courses abroad may count)
test_out: Not stated for WOL. Foreign language courses taken on a term abroad automatically count for WOL. No placement, AP/IB, high-school-years or native-speaker exemption is described.
notes: Current general education is the Complex Questions curriculum (students entering fall 2022 and later). Catalog: 'Students entering in the Fall of 2025 and later are required to take eight Perspectives courses' from eight Perspectives (CAD, CHF, DQR, ETS, LIT, NPS, SPE, WOL), with at least one G and one J Area-of-Inquiry course, 'but you decide how to distribute the Perspectives'; the catalog does not say one course in each Perspective is required, so WOL is not an explicit universal requirement. Sources conflict: Union's gen-ed website says 'Every Union student takes seven courses from a range of eight Perspectives' (classes of 2026-27: six), which clearly makes WOL optional, while union.edu/academic/complex-questions says 'every student will be exposed to at least one course in each of the following academic Perspectives' for the fully implemented curriculum (class of 2028+). If the eight-courses/eight-Perspectives reading is applied, one term of language becomes effectively required for students entering fall 2025 and later. The older Common Curriculum (pre-fall 2022) had a Languages and Cultures (LCC) requirement satisfiable by two language courses OR two non-language LCC culture courses OR a term abroad (https://catalog.union.edu/content.php?catoid=29&navoid=1340). Gen-ed site: https://www.union.edu/gen-ed/students-advisors/advising-guidelines , https://www.union.edu/gen-ed/curriculum.

applies_to: students in menu option: every undergraduate must complete one Language and Culture Perspective (LP) course, which may be a language course or a literature/culture course other than English
level_required: Language and Culture Perspective: 'Develop intercultural literacy through the study of a language or literature other than English' (one LP-designated course, any level; no proficiency level specified). Department of Language, Literature and Culture: 'Although there is no language requirement at Clark, every student is expected to take at least one course that deals with the interrelation between language and culture.'
test_out: Not stated. Clark's curriculum pages describe no placement, AP/IB, high-school-years or native-speaker exemption for the LP perspective; the LP course is a one-course distribution requirement rather than a proficiency requirement.
notes: Clark Core (fall 2024 and later): First-Year Intensive plus nine requirements across five disciplines (Aesthetic, Scientific, Global Comparative, History, Language and Culture, Values, Diversity and Inclusion, Written Expression, Formal Analysis), Problems of Practice, and a Capstone. The LP learning outcome ('demonstrate basic speaking, listening, reading, writing and intercultural skills in a language/culture other than English/American', per the Clark Core learning goals PDF) is language-oriented, but Clark's Language, Literature and Culture department states explicitly that there is no language requirement and that LP can be met by a course on the interrelation of language and culture (e.g., literature in translation courses taught in English). Students who entered before fall 2024 follow the Program of Liberal Studies, which had the same one-course LP Perspective. Supporting pages: https://www.clarku.edu/language-literature-and-culture/academics/courses/ , https://clarku.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/clark-core-learning-goals.pdf , https://www.clarku.edu/academics/undergraduate-curriculum/program-of-liberal-studies/ . The 2026-27 catalog (catalog.clarku.edu, catoid=37) exists but its content pages returned empty to the fetcher.

segment: More than one year, all students
applies_to: all undergraduates (listed among the general education requirements for the bachelor's degree with no exemptions stated)
level_required: 'Foreign Language (1 course)'; footnote: 'Depending on language placement, students may take one to two prerequisites before completing the 200-level foreign language requirement.' I.e., one course at the 200 level (third-semester / intermediate).
test_out: Not stated in the catalog's graduation-requirements list; placement determines how many prerequisite courses (0-2) precede the required 200-level course. The catalog's detailed 'Foreign Language' subsection could not be rendered by the fetcher (JavaScript-driven page), so any AP/IB, placement-exam or native-speaker exemption could not be confirmed. An older Drew Chinese-program page states that an AP Chinese score of 4 or 5 is 'considered to have fulfilled the College's general education language requirement' and that the placement exam can exempt students from the first two courses (https://depts.drew.edu/chin/program.htm); treat as indicative only.
notes: Drew general education: Drew Seminar or College Writing (1); Breadth of Knowledge (5: natural science, social science, humanities, arts, interdisciplinary); Writing (3); Quantitative Literacy (2); Foreign Language (1, at the 200 level); Engaging Difference (2: Global Challenges; Power, Privilege and Difference); Immersive Experiences (2). The requirement is framed as one 200-level course, but a student with no prior background takes two 100-level prerequisites first, so three semesters total. The same text appears in the archived 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26 catalogs (e.g., https://archive-drew-undergraduate-25-26.catalog.prod.coursedog.com/quicklinks/graduationrequirements). General education page: https://drew-undergraduate-catalog.coursedog.com/quicklinks/gened.

applies_to: none (requirement discontinued)
level_required: none; the catalog page states 'SPU has discontinued its Foreign Language Competency requirement' effective Spring 2025 for all current and future students
test_out: n/a
notes: Until Spring 2025 SPU required Foreign Language Competency for every bachelor's degree (C or pass in the second quarter of an elementary SPU language course or higher; or two years of one high-school language with a C average; Seal of Biliteracy; AP/IB/Cambridge credit; approved WA/OR/CA direct-transfer degree; transferred course; ASL; native/near-native proficiency; CLEP; ACTFL Intermediate-Low oral proficiency; or approved immersion program). The 2026-27 catalog's Baccalaureate Degree Requirements checklist (Common Curriculum + Exploratory Curriculum 'Ways of Knowing' + Cultural Understanding and Engagement) contains no language requirement; the legacy competency page now carries only the discontinuation notice. SPU also disbanded its Languages, Cultures and Linguistics department in 2025 (student newspaper, Feb 2024), retaining only elementary language courses as electives/gen-ed options.

applies_to: students in menu option (all undergraduates must complete the 'Language and Intercultural Competence' general education area, but a language course is only one way to satisfy it)
level_required: 'LANGUAGE AND INTERCULTURAL COMPETENCE (one course required)' - any one course from the approved list; language options include ASL 101/102/201/202, SPAN 101/102/201/202/205/208W, LATN 101/102/103/105/201W/202W/205W/208W, but non-language courses (e.g., INTL 213, INTL 301, MGMT 303, ENGL 323, HIST 275, POLI 260, PSYC 231, COMM 251) also satisfy it
test_out: Waiver available for students whose native language is not English (substitution waiver form with documentation of native-language proficiency submitted to the Department of Modern and Classical Languages); international students from non-English-speaking countries may waive with documentation of International Student status. No placement-exam, AP/IB, or high-school-years test-out is stated for the general education area.
notes: Lynchburg's DELL ('Diverse, Engaged, Lifelong Learners') general education requires every student, regardless of major, to take one course in the Language and Intercultural Competence area under Goal 3 (Exploring Global Perspectives and Expanding Social Responsibility); the catalog describes it as 'at least one intercultural competency course that explores cultures, perspectives, and practices that differ from their own.' A single 101-level language course counts, so semesters_equivalent is 1 only if a student chooses the language route; the requirement can be met with no language study at all. No separate BA-vs-BS foreign-language requirement was found. Westover Honors students follow a separate honors sequence. The online catalog (catalog.lynchburg.edu) blocks fetching, so the university's official 2025-26 catalog PDF was used; the 2026-27 catalog was not located.

applies_to: students in menu option (College of Arts and Sciences students pick 5 of 6 'Knowledge of Human Cultures and the Natural World' areas, one of which is Modern Languages; School of Business students have Modern Language as one option in two menus)
level_required: College of Arts and Sciences: 'Modern Languages (any L course)' - 1 unit; 'Select five of the following' six areas, '1 unit each from 5 out of the 6 areas'. test_out: Not stated for the general education area (it can simply be avoided by choosing other areas). Placement policy: students with two or more years of high-school study in a language they wish to continue must take a placement exam; four years of high-school study places at the 102 level or higher. AP/IB credit rules for languages are not stated.

applies_to: College of Arts and Sciences students (all majors in CAS); not required by the University Core for other colleges
level_required: Competency through the 1350 level, demonstrated by completing the 'three-course language sequence - 1150, 1250, and 1350' (three quarters of first-year college language) or placing beyond it
test_out: Placement into a higher course via an oral exam or the Modern Language Competency Examination (placement does not earn credit); 15 credits of American Sign Language or documented ASL fluency; native non-English speakers who completed schooling through age 16 in a non-English language of instruction or earned an acceptable TOEFL score; students with documented learning disabilities may substitute 15 credits of approved international/cross-cultural courses (the Core FAQ says only UCOR 3100, 3400, 3600 and 3800 may serve as Foreign Language Substitution courses). High-school years and AP are not mentioned in the policy.
notes: Seattle University is on the quarter system; three quarters (1150-1250-1350) equal one academic year, roughly two semesters. The University Core FAQ (2026-27) states 'The University Core Curriculum does not have a foreign language requirement' but that 'some colleges and programs do require proficiency in a language'. The CAS requirement is set in Registrar policy 87-01 'Performance Criteria for Undergraduates in the College of Arts and Sciences' (last revised 12/2022). The Core FAQ also notes that for students entering 2027-28 or later a language course above the college's language requirement can fulfill UCOR 3200 Global Perspectives (CAS majors at level 2150 or above; other majors 1150 or above), implicitly confirming the CAS requirement ends at 1350. The acalog catalog pages (catalog.seattleu.edu, catoid=61) returned no readable content, so the registrar policy PDF and the official Core FAQ were used; a North Seattle College transfer guide (third party, revised 7/2025) corroborates: 'All students with majors in the College of Arts and Sciences need three quarters of college-level language' and high-school credits do not satisfy it.

applies_to: students in certain College of Arts and Sciences BA majors only (e.g., English, History, Philosophy, Religious Studies, Sociology, Criminology & Justice); not a Loyola Core or university-wide requirement
level_required: Where required by the major: '6 crs of language credit, up to the 201 level of proficiency' (e.g., 'English majors are required to complete 6 crs of language credit, up to the 201 level of proficiency'); students who place into 201 need only 3 crs
test_out: Placement activity required to begin the language sequence; placing into the 201 level reduces the requirement to 3 credits (the other 3 credits become general electives). No AP/IB thresholds or high-school-year rules are stated in the bulletin program pages.
notes: The Loyola Core (42 credit hours across 14 areas: First-Year Seminar, English Composition, Mathematics, Science, Creative Arts & Cultures, History 1 and 2, Natural Science in Context, Philosophy 1 and 2, Religious Studies - Christian Traditions and World Religions, Social Science, Writing About Literature) contains no language requirement, and the CAS 'Regulations on Degree Completion' list no college-wide language rule. Language appears only as an 'adjunct' requirement in specific major programs (6 credits 'up to the 201 level'; teacher-education tracks reduce it to 3 credits), so a student in, e.g., Political Science, Business, Music or Nursing has no language requirement. The 6-credit requirement is written so that a student with no background takes two courses that end before 201 (i.e., 100-101), so semesters_equivalent is 2; classical languages (Latin, Greek) qualify. Major pages consulted: https://2026bulletin.loyno.edu/undergraduate/cas/humanities and https://2026bulletin.loyno.edu/undergraduate/cas/social-sciences.

applies_to: all undergraduates subject to the Undergraduate Core (BA/BS students in the College of Arts and Sciences); the Core does not apply to the Bachelor of Education, Bachelor of Health Science, Dental Hygiene, Bachelor of Applied Vision Science or BS in Vision Science completion/professional programs
level_required: 'Students must complete a 102-level language course or higher or demonstrate equivalent proficiency' (Language is one of the five Foundations requirements of the Undergraduate Core)
test_out: Language Placement Test (placement into 102 or higher means taking only the course placed into); STAMP4s proficiency exam at a level equivalent to 102 ($50, may take twice); AP language exam score of 4 or higher (grants 102-level credit and satisfies the requirement); IB Higher Level 5 or higher (satisfies; IB Standard Level 5 earns 4 credits but does not satisfy); transfer credit for a 102-level or higher semester course (103+ quarter) with C- or better (Latin excluded); petition for exemption with 4+ years of high-school study (B or better) in a language not taught at Pacific; automatic exemption for international students who took university-level ESL; petitions for students with 6+ years of schooling in a non-English language, native speakers of other languages, heritage speakers, or K-12 immersion graduates; general petition to waive for students fluent in reading, writing and speaking a language other than English.
notes: Pacific revised its Undergraduate Core in 2018-19; Foundations = First Year Experience, Math, Writing, Language, International and Diverse Perspectives; Explorations = 4 credits in each of six modes of inquiry; Applications = Civic Engagement, Sustainability, Senior Capstone. A student starting a new language takes 101 and 102 (two semesters). Languages offered: ASL, French, Japanese, Spanish. The 2026-27 acalog catalog page 'Baccalaureate Core & Other Graduation Requirements' (https://catalog.pacificu.edu/content.php?catoid=20&navoid=1182) returned no readable content, so the university's official core-requirements pages (https://www.pacificu.edu/academics/undergraduate-curriculum/core-requirements and the Language Proficiency Options page https://pacificu.edu/node/38276) were used.

segment: More than one year, all students
applies_to: all undergraduates (all students except native speakers/writers of a language other than English who document proficiency)
level_required: Completion of the Foreign Language & Culture Goucher Commons Requirement (FLC GCR) 'platform' set by placement: Platform 1 (placed in 110) = 110 + 120 + 130 or 132 (10 credits); Platform 2 (placed in 120) = 120 + 130 (8 credits); Platform 3 (placed in 130) = 130 + one 200-level course (8 credits); Platform 4 (placed beyond 130) = one 200- or 300-level course (4 credits). I.e., a beginner must complete through the 130 (intermediate) level.
test_out: Placement test required of everyone before enrolling (results expire after one year); higher placement reduces the platform to as little as one 200/300-level course, but every non-exempt student must still pass at least one course at Goucher or an accredited institution. Native speakers/foreign nationals may be exempted with proof such as a high-school diploma from a school where English is not the primary language or a teacher/faculty attestation; heritage speakers are not considered native speakers and must consult the department chair. An AP score alone does not earn Spanish credit or satisfy the requirement; students must take the placement exam (no AP/IB thresholds stated). Transfer credit may count but the terminal course of the platform must be passed at Goucher or a regionally accredited college. ASL accepted via 4-12 credits at another accredited institution with an approved plan.
notes: The Goucher Commons curriculum (First-Year Seminar, two Complex Problem Explorations, justice/environmental inquiry areas, study abroad for all students, writing proficiency 3-course sequence, data analytics 2-course sequence, foreign language and culture proficiency, capstone) states that 'all students are expected to meet cultural awareness and language-specific learning outcomes'. Grade rules: C- or better in 110 and 120; D acceptable in the final course of the sequence; audits and 100-level independent study do not count. Students should begin in the first year and generally not take the final course in the senior year. Languages not offered at Goucher require MLLC chair approval (e.g., via BSEP). The 2026-27 acalog catalog (goucher.catalog.acalog.com) pages returned no readable content and its search is blocked, so the college's official curriculum page describing the FLC GCR was used; the placement-exams page (https://www.goucher.edu/become/new-students/placement-exams) corroborates the exemption rules.

level_required: "Students must demonstrate Level 2 proficiency in a language other than English"; i.e., completion of "the second semester-long course in the same language sequence" (old Core, pre-Fall 2022, required Level 3)
test_out: Three years of the same non-English language in high school (including ASL) with a grade of C- or better; AP language exam score of 3 or higher; IB higher-level language exam score of 5 or higher; pass a proctored proficiency exam approved by World Languages and Cultures or Classical Languages (Avant placement test at intermediate level, confirmed by oral/written proficiency testing); TOEFL meeting enrollment standards for international non-native English speakers; transfer of the second-semester course from an accredited institution. applies_to: candidates for the Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Science degrees (B.A. and B.S.) must complete one of three options, one of which is non-language; B.A. majors in English and Global Studies must take the language Option I; other bachelor's degrees (e.g., BBA, BSN, BFA, BMus, BAE) are not covered

test_out: Option I: four years of high school study in one language with grades of C or higher, or a passing score on a proficiency exam given by the PLU Department of Languages and Literatures. notes: Menu structure: language is required only if the student does not choose Option III (non-language). Minimum language path (Option II) is one year (2 semesters); Option I is two years (4 semesters). semesters_equivalent=2 reflects the minimum language option; 0 if the student chooses Option III.
